q: A fundus with tortuous, dilated, dark veins and a blood-and-thunder pattern of hemorrhages indicates:
w: Engorged tortuous veins with widespread hemorrhages is the blood-and-thunder fundus of CRVO. Artery occlusion instead makes the retina pale.
k: Tortuous dark veins, blood and thunder = CRVO.

q: Arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, a retinal sheen from edema, and hard exudates describe:
w: Narrowed arterioles with AV nicking, edema, and hard exudates are hypertensive retinopathy. Arteriosclerotic change instead shows copper or silver wiring.
k: Narrowing plus sheen and exudates = hypertensive.

q: Lipid plaques within the retinal arterial wall with vascular sheathing (copper or silver wiring) describe:
w: Wall lipid with sheathing and copper or silver wiring is arteriosclerotic retinopathy. Hypertensive retinopathy centers on edema and exudates.
k: Copper or silver wire = arteriosclerotic.

q: Serous macular edema from a pigment-epithelium leak in a young adult describes:
w: A localized serous macular detachment from an RPE leak in a young patient is central serous chorioretinopathy. The others are diffuse vascular retinopathies.
k: Young adult, serous macular leak = central serous.

q: Microaneurysms, dot-and-blot hemorrhages, and neovascularization describe:
w: Microaneurysms, dot-and-blot hemorrhages, and later neovascularization are the hallmark of diabetic retinopathy.
k: Microaneurysms = diabetic retinopathy.

q: Bone-spicule pigmentation, attenuated vessels, and a waxy pale disc describe:
w: Bone-spicule pigment with attenuated vessels and a waxy pale disc, plus night blindness, is retinitis pigmentosa.
k: Bone spicules and waxy disc = retinitis pigmentosa.

q: An acute anterior uveitis with fibrin in the anterior chamber in a young patient is characteristic of:
w: Acute anterior uveitis with anterior-chamber fibrin in a young patient points to rheumatoid disease. TB uveitis is granulomatous with mutton-fat precipitates.
k: Fibrin plus young patient = rheumatoid uveitis.

q: A granulomatous uveitis with whitish nodules in the iris is characteristic of:
w: Granulomatous uveitis with whitish iris nodules is characteristic of leprosy. Rheumatoid uveitis is non-granulomatous with fibrin.
k: Granulomatous iris nodules = leprosy.

q: A protean uveitis with greasy mutton-fat keratic precipitates and iris nodules is characteristic of:
w: A variable granulomatous uveitis with greasy mutton-fat precipitates and iris nodules is characteristic of tuberculosis.
k: Mutton-fat precipitates, protean = tuberculosis.

q: Glaucoma in which aqueous reaches the angle at all times with no other ocular or systemic disease is:
w: An open angle with no other cause is primary open-angle glaucoma. Secondary types have a precipitating disease; angle-closure types have a blocked angle.
k: Open angle, no other disease = POAG.

q: Posterior synechiae that block aqueous flow produce which glaucoma?
w: Posterior synechiae are an acquired cause that closes the angle, giving secondary angle-closure glaucoma. Primary types have no precipitating disease.
k: Synechiae close the angle = secondary angle closure.

q: Which procedure is NOT a treatment for glaucoma?
w: Goniotomy, trabeculectomy, and fistulizing operations lower intraocular pressure. Capsulectomy is a lens-capsule procedure, not a glaucoma surgery.
k: Capsulectomy is a lens procedure, not glaucoma surgery.

q: Which condition does NOT cause congenital glaucoma?
w: Axenfeld syndrome, aniridia, and Sturge-Weber syndrome all cause congenital glaucoma. Diabetes does not.
k: Diabetes does not cause congenital glaucoma.

q: Iris strands attached to a prominent Schwalbe line (posterior embryotoxon) with a glaucoma risk describe:
w: Iris strands to a prominent Schwalbe line (posterior embryotoxon) with glaucoma risk is Axenfeld syndrome. Peters anomaly instead is a central corneal opacity.
k: Strands to Schwalbe line = Axenfeld.

q: A central corneal opacity with a defect in the posterior stroma, Descemet membrane, and endothelium describes:
w: A central corneal opacity with a posterior stromal, Descemet, and endothelial defect is Peters anomaly. Axenfeld affects the angle and iris strands.
k: Central corneal opacity, Descemet defect = Peters.

q: Spherophakia, an abnormally round crystalline lens, typically produces:
w: A rounder lens adds plus power and shifts the eye toward lenticular myopia. A notched lens (coloboma) instead throws astigmatism.
k: Round lens adds power = myopia.

q: A coloboma of the crystalline lens most commonly produces:
w: A notched or tilted lens gives uneven refraction, so a lens coloboma throws astigmatism. A uniformly rounder lens instead causes myopia.
k: Notched lens = astigmatism.

q: A first-trimester maternal viral infection classically causing congenital cataract is:
w: Rubella in the first trimester classically causes congenital cataract, plus heart and hearing defects. The others are not the classic cause.
k: First-trimester congenital cataract = rubella.

q: Conjunctivitis resulting from mishandling of contact lenses is:
w: Chronic mechanical and immune irritation from contact lenses causes giant papillary conjunctivitis. Pseudomonas instead causes contact-lens keratitis.
k: Contact-lens mishandling = giant papillary conjunctivitis.

q: The most common cause of bacterial conjunctivitis is:
w: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common bacterial conjunctivitis. Pseudomonas is the contact-lens keratitis organism.
k: Commonest bacterial conjunctivitis = S. aureus.

q: Conjunctivitis with intense itching and a thick discharge triggered by cosmetics or eye medications is:
w: A reaction to drugs, cosmetics, or eye drops on the ocular surface is contact conjunctivitis. Allergic conjunctivitis is more seasonal and airborne-triggered.
k: Drug or cosmetic trigger = contact conjunctivitis.

q: A corneal opacity that is dense and totally opaque is a:
w: The opacity ladder runs nebula (faint) to macula (moderate) to leukoma (dense, totally opaque).
k: Totally opaque cornea = leukoma.
